disposition_reason: Field trial of surface compost at two rates versus control on four Ecuadorian cacao farms, reporting soil Cd fractionation, humic/fulvic-acid-bound Cd, pH and SOC by treatment, and only correlation coefficients between soil pools and leaf/bean Cd. Unfermented bean Cd was measured but no bean (or leaf) Cd concentrations are printed by farm or treatment, so there are no occurrence findings; the extractable content is soil-level mitigation evidence plus correlations.

study.design: field trial (randomized complete block, 3 replicates per farm, 3 treatments)
study.material_scope: cacao-farm soil (0-5 and 5-20 cm), cacao leaves, unfermented unpeeled oven-dried beans from ripe pods
study.growing_origin_vs_market: Grown on four farms in Ecuador: farms 1-3 Manabí, farm 4 Guayas; no market products
study.sampling_unit: plot of 21 trees, 5 central trees sampled; 3 replicate plots per treatment per farm
study.method: Beans and leaves: HNO3 digestion, ICP-OES (farms 1-3) or microwave digestion and ICP-MS (farm 4); soil total Cd aqua regia, ICP-OES; sequential fractions GFAAS (H2O and EDTA by ICP-MS)
study.lod_loq: PQL: ICP-OES 24 µg Cd/L, GFAAS 0.6 µg Cd/L, ICP-MS 0.6 µg Cd/L (solution basis)
study.basis: beans oven-dried 65 °C 72 h (dry weight); soil air-dried
study.qa: CRMs NIST 2709a soil (80.1 ± 0.05%), NIST 1573a leaves (96.4 ± 0.03%; 92.9 ± 3.70% farm 4), FDA-CP36 cacao beans (98.3 ± 0.01%) not used for farm 4, NIST 2384 baking chocolate for farm 4 (91.5 ± 10.2%); duplicate CV beans 1.29-2.80%

controls.control: Surface compost application (low rate; Methods: 6.25 Mg/ha/yr, table footnotes: 12.5 Mg/ha/yr) within 1 m of trunk after removing litter; commercial compost 62% OM, pH >= 6.16, Cd 0.03 mg/kg
controls.comparator: no-compost control plots, farm 1 (Manabí, Ecuador), applied once, soil sampled 3 months and beans 12 months after application; n=3 replicate plots, mean ± SE; * = Dunnett p<0.05
controls.outcome: 0-5 cm: humic-acid-bound Cd 1.35±0.5 -> 2.25±0.8 µg/kg; fulvic-acid-bound Cd 11.2±0.2 -> 12.4±0.5 µg/kg; pH 7.7 -> 7.2; SOC 1.37 -> 1.96 %; 5-20 cm: humic-acid-bound Cd 0.41±0.2 -> 0.43±0.1 µg/kg; fulvic-acid-bound Cd 7.65±0.4 -> 7.97±1.8 µg/kg; pH 7.2 -> 6.8; SOC 0.70 -> 0.89 %. controls.control: Surface compost application: redistribution of labile soil Cd (KNO3/H2O-extractable)
controls.outcome: Farm 1: KNO3/H2O-Cd 1.54-fold lower with low rate at 0-5 cm (p<0.05) and 1.44-fold lower with high rate at 5-20 cm; farm 4: high rate 1.13- and 1.11-fold lower at the two depths. NaOH-bound Cd ~3-fold (3.32-fold) higher with high rate at farm 4; EDTA-Cd 4- and 3.8-fold higher (farm 1, low/high) and 1.6- and 1.8-fold higher (farm 4). HNO3-Cd unchanged. Values only in Figures 2-4 (text fold-changes).
controls.locator: Results 'Cadmium pools affected by organic matter application', PDF pp.5-6; Figures 2-4

controls.control: Increase soil Cd bound to fulvic acid / soil organic carbon (via high-fulvic-acid compost) as a bean-Cd mitigation pathway
controls.comparator: correlation across all plots and four farms
controls.outcome: Bean Cd correlations (surface 0-5 cm / below surface 5-20 cm): Cd-FA r = -0.31 / -0.32 (single star, which the source legend defines as p<0.1); SOC r = -0.39 / -0.38 (p<0.05); Cd-HNO3 r = -0.50 / -0.52 (p<0.05); Cd-NaOH r = -0.23 (ns) / -0.29 (p<0.1); Cd-HA r = +0.36 (p<0.05) / +0.06; Cd-EDTA r = +0.37 (p<0.05) / -0.26 (ns). Bean Cd vs Leaf-Cd1 r = 0.66, vs Leaf-Cd2 r = 0.41.

context_notes: Total soil Cd across the four farms ranged 0.37 to 0.92 mg/kg; all clay soils.
Authors note a 0.6 mg/kg dry-weight bean Cd threshold that may impair commercialization (cited, not a regulation in this paper).
contradictions_with_stored_summary: Stored summary says cacao-bean recovery was 98.3% against FDA-CP36 'across all farms'; the primary says the CRMs (including FDA-CP36) were used except for farm 4, which used NIST 2384.
Stored summary explains the 12.5/25 Mg/ha/yr table labels as due to farm 4 receiving two applications; the primary gives no such explanation (the conflict is unexplained).

Stored summary says the humic- and fulvic-acid fractions were quantified by GFAAS; the primary states only that 'the different soil fractions (except H2O and EDTA)' were quantified by GFAAS and does not name the instrument for HA/FA explicitly.
Stored summary characterises the abstract claim that leaf and bean Cd were negatively correlated with EDTA-extractable Cd without noting that Tables 4-5 contradict it for beans.
integrity_issues: Compost rates: Methods and abstract give 6.25 (low) and 12.5 (high) Mg/ha per annum; Table 2 and 3 footnotes give 12.5 and 25 Mg/ha per year.

Discussion states compost increased soil pH by 0.2 units on average at both depths, but Table 2 shows lower mean pH in compost plots at farms 1-3 (e.g. farm 1 surface 7.7 control vs 6.6 high rate); only farm 4 low rate increased (significantly).

Abstract says leaf and bean Cd were negatively and significantly correlated with EDTA-extractable Cd, but Table 4 gives bean-Cd vs Cd-EDTA r = +0.37 (p<0.05) and leaf r = +0.36, and Table 5 gives bean r = -0.26 (ns).
Correlation-table legend defines '*p < 0.1' as 'statistically significant', a non-standard threshold; claims of significant bean-Cd vs Cd-FA correlation rest on p<0.1.
unresolved: Bean and leaf Cd concentrations by farm and treatment are not printed in the paper; the data availability statement says raw data are available from the authors on request. No bean-level mitigation effect size can be extracted.
Calendar dates of compost application and sampling are not reported.
Fraction concentrations for KNO3/H2O, NaOH, EDTA and HNO3 pools are shown only in figures; only text fold-changes are extracted.
